extracted.intended_audience: journalism and English composition educators; researchers in journalism education; curriculum planners
extracted.subtask_description: Survey-based research investigating journalism students' perceptions of freshman English composition as preparation for news writing, including which course skills are emphasized and which student/instructional variables predict success in introductory journalism courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: writing concisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write concisely (one of 11 skills students were asked to rate for how well composition and journalism courses taught it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by the authors as a 'practical skill' (part of the practical skills set journalism is expected to teach). Survey findings: journalism tended to be rated higher than composition on concision at SMSU and SDSU; included in ranked comparisons and mean-difference analyses (Tables 7-9, Table 8 shows concisely often among top differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: writing precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write precisely (one of the 11 evaluated skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a 'practical skill.' Students rated how well each course taught precision; comparisons and correlations between courses reported (means, rank correlations).

rubrics_metrics.name: writing clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write clearly (one of the 11 evaluated skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized in the literature review as a central trait of good journalistic writing ('good journalistic writing is clear and simple'); measured and compared between composition and journalism courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: organized writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write in an organized manner (one of the 11 evaluated skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among practical skills and appeared among top-ranked skills in student ratings at both institutions; used in correlational comparisons of course emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: correct grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of correct grammar (one of the 11 evaluated skills and a focal point of debate in composition instruction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a practical, work-world-oriented skill; the paper reports how much grammar instruction students recalled receiving, discusses literature on effectiveness of grammar instruction, and compares course ratings for grammar (noting differences by institution and course).

rubrics_metrics.name: correct spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of correct spelling (one of the 11 evaluated skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured via student ratings and via questions about instructor strictness in grading for spelling; identified in ASNE findings as high priority for editors (spelling ranked near top).

rubrics_metrics.name: writing for one's audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write for an audience (one of the 11 evaluated skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as a practical skill and noted as the skill most similarly taught in composition and journalism (students rated 'audience' as the most similar between the two courses).

rubrics_metrics.name: writing interestingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write in an interesting way (one of the 11 evaluated skills; part of 'reflective skills').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by the authors as a reflective skill (contrasted with practical skills); students rated how well courses taught this skill and comparisons reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: writing creatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write creatively (one of the 11 evaluated skills; categorized as a reflective skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note composition often emphasizes creativity; authors contrasted creative/expressive emphasis with journalism's practical emphasis and reported student ratings (journalism generally rated lower on creativity).

rubrics_metrics.name: writing in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to write in detail (one of the 11 evaluated skills; reflective skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in the reflective skills set; student ratings for detail were compared across courses and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: using one's own opinions in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to use one's own opinions in writing (one of the 11 evaluated skills; reflective skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by the authors as a reflective skill; student ratings showed composition emphasized this more than journalism at times (reported in means/rankings).

rubrics_metrics.name: overall value of freshman composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' overall rating of how valuable the writing instruction in their first freshman English composition course was (survey question #1, 1–5 scale combined into low/high).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized as percentage reporting 'quite a bit' or 'very much' valuable; reported by institution and cross-tabulated with independent variables (composition grade, ACT, sex, major). Findings: minority rated high value overall; associations with A in courses noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: usefulness of freshman composition in the work world
rubrics_metrics.description: Student-rated usefulness of freshman composition for writing in the work world (survey question #2, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported as percent 'quite a bit'/'very much'; analyzed by institution and independent variables. Overall only ~29.9% rated composition as highly useful for the work world; SMSU students more likely than SDSU to rate usefulness high.

rubrics_metrics.name: usefulness of freshman composition for other academic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Student-rated usefulness of freshman composition for other academic writing (survey question #3, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nearly half (~46.8%) rated it high; differences by institution and by composition grade reported; one significant relationship: SDSU students with an A in composition more likely to rate it useful for other academic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: usefulness of freshman composition for journalistic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Student-rated usefulness of freshman composition for journalistic writing (survey question #4, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only ~23.4% rated it high; analyzed by institution and independent variables; SDSU A students more likely to find it useful, SMSU patterns differed.

rubrics_metrics.name: amount of grammar instruction in freshman composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Student recall of how much grammar instruction they received in their first freshman composition course (survey question #5, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported that only ~19.5% reported 'quite a bit' or 'very much' grammar instruction in freshman comp; used as an independent variable in prediction analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: amount of high school grammar instruction (10th–12th grades)
rubrics_metrics.description: Student recall of how much grammar instruction they received in high school English classes (survey question #6, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately 64.9% reported 'quite a bit' or 'very much' in high school; used to examine relationships with college course success.

rubrics_metrics.name: strictness grading for grammar in freshman composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Student perception of how strict the freshman composition instructor was in grading writing for grammar mistakes (survey question #7, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About 46.8% reported the instructor was 'quite' or 'very' strict; included as part of 'previous instruction' variable in predictive models.

rubrics_metrics.name: strictness grading for spelling in freshman composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Student perception of how strict the freshman composition instructor was in grading writing for spelling mistakes (survey question #8, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About 64.6% reported 'quite' or 'very' strict; used in analyses and as part of prior instruction measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: student liking of freshman composition course
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the student liked their first freshman composition course (survey question #9, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported percent liking the course; used descriptively and in cross-tabs with other variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: student liking of writing portions of introductory journalism course
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the student liked the writing portions of their introductory journalism writing course (survey question #10, 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMSU students liked journalism writing portions more than SDSU (70.5% vs 40.6% 'quite a bit'/'very much'); used to compare attitudes toward the two courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: perceived time devoted to writing vs literature in freshman composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Student opinion on whether enough class time was devoted to writing relative to literature in freshman composition (survey question #11; response options include 'not enough').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About 24.7% said 'not enough'; analyzed by institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: perceived time devoted to writing vs non-writing topics in journalism course
rubrics_metrics.description: Student opinion on whether enough class time was devoted to writing in the introductory journalism course compared to non-writing topics (survey question #12; response options include 'not enough').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only ~11.9% said 'not enough'; used to contrast course emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: English ACT score as predictor of success
rubrics_metrics.description: English ACT score (categorized high = 23+ vs low = 22 and under) used as an independent variable to predict success (A grade) in introductory journalism and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: higher English ACT score was significantly associated with receiving an A in journalism overall and in SDSU; English ACT also related to A in composition (statistically significant overall).

rubrics_metrics.name: composite ACT score as predictor of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite ACT score (categorized high = 23+ vs low = 22 and under) used to predict course success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high composite ACT score was significantly associated with receiving an A in the introductory journalism course overall and at both institutions; also associated with A in composition in some analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: freshman composition grade as predictor of journalism success
rubrics_metrics.description: Letter grade in the first freshman composition course (A vs non-A) considered as a predictor of success (A grade) in introductory journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesized to be the best predictor but results were mixed: composition grade predicted whether students valued composition and its usefulness for other academic writing, and at SDSU a high composition grade predicted a high journalism grade, but not at SMSU; overall not consistently the best predictor.

rubrics_metrics.name: student sex (gender) as predictor of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Student sex (male/female) included as an independent variable to predict A grades and perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: males were more likely to have received an A in journalism (statistically significant overall and at SDSU); differences in perceptions by sex were noted across institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: print journalism major status as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether student declared a print journalism major (vs non-print major) included as an independent variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print majors were somewhat more likely to receive As in journalism and to rate composition value differently; not always statistically significant (small sample).

rubrics_metrics.name: previous grammar and spelling instruction as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of previous grammar and spelling instruction (in high school and freshman composition) and perceived strictness of grading, combined into a 'previous instruction' predictor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by authors; previous instruction was a good predictor only for journalism grade in their analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: classification: practical skills vs reflective skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' categorical rubric dividing skills into 'practical skills' (concise, precise, clear, organized, grammar, spelling, audience) and 'reflective skills' (interesting, creative, in detail, opinions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to form hypotheses (journalism teaches practical skills; composition teaches reflective skills). Practical skills were explicitly defined in the paper; reflective skills likewise were defined; comparisons and hypothesis tests used this taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: good journalistic writing is clear and simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative criterion argued in the literature review: 'good journalistic writing is clear and simple' (Mencher; supported by findings like editors ranking writing, spelling, and grammar as top skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a background evaluative standard: the ASNE study cited editors ranking writing skills, spelling and grammar as most important for new hires (with low percentages rating applicants as strong), supporting the study's focus on practical skills and work-world relevance.
